inconclusive.n: Used mainly in science, medicine, law and journalism for evidence or tests that fail to settle a question. It is neutral: it does not say the result was negative, only that it did not prove anything either way. Typical partners are results, evidence, findings, talks and debate. The opposite is conclusive, and the adverb is inconclusively. Stress falls on the second syllable: in-con-CLU-sive.
x: The police said the DNA evidence was inconclusive and released the suspect.
After two days of inconclusive talks, both sides agreed to meet again next month.

launch a campaign.n: A fixed collocation: you launch a campaign when it officially begins, whether it is advertising, a political push or a charity appeal. The campaign is usually for something (to raise awareness, to promote a product) or against something. Launch sounds more dynamic than start and fits news and business writing well. Common adjectives: a national, nationwide or social media campaign. Run, wage and mount are related verbs; wage and mount suit campaigns against a problem.
x: The charity plans to launch a campaign against plastic waste in the spring.
Before she can launch a campaign for mayor, she needs funding and volunteers.

muggy.n: Describes weather that is warm, damp and still, so the air feels heavy and sweat does not dry. It is informal and mostly about weather, and it is stronger than just humid, which can be a neutral measurement. People say it is muggy, a muggy afternoon or hot and muggy. It is common in British and American speech alike. A muggy day often ends with a thunderstorm, and the noun is mugginess.
x: It was so muggy last night that I could not sleep without the fan on.
Ho Chi Minh City can feel muggy even after the rain stops.

seismic.n: The adjective belonging to earthquakes: seismic waves, seismic activity, a seismic zone. In science it is literal and precise, and the study of earthquakes is seismology. Journalists also use it figuratively for a huge, far-reaching change, as in a seismic shift in politics, where it signals a dramatic effect rather than a physical tremor. It is pronounced SIZE-mik. Compare tectonic, which concerns the movement of plates themselves.
x: Engineers must design bridges in this region to resist seismic forces.
The election result caused a seismic shift in the country's politics.

staple.n: Three senses share one spelling. The adjective means basic and always present: staple food, staple crop, staple diet, the items a population eats every day, such as rice, maize or bread. The noun a staple (of something) is a basic, regular item, as in comedy was a staple of Saturday television. A separate noun is the small metal fastener used with paper. Do not use it for something merely popular for a short time.
x: Cassava is the staple crop in many parts of tropical Africa.
Pasta has been a staple of the Italian diet for centuries.

sign up for.n: A phrasal verb meaning to put your name down to join a course, club, newsletter or service. The preposition for introduces what you join, while sign up alone can stand without an object: Did you sign up? It is inseparable here, since sign up for is followed directly by the thing joined. In formal writing, register for or enrol in is more usual. Do not confuse it with sign in, which means to log in to an account.
x: Did you sign up for the marathon yet? Places are filling quickly.
You can sign up for the library newsletter to hear about new books.

underlie.n: A formal verb meaning to be the hidden basis or cause of something visible. It is irregular: underlie, underlay, underlain, underlying. Underlay is its past tense, so it should not be confused with the noun. It is much more common in its adjective form underlying, as in the underlying causes, and its subject is usually an abstract idea, a principle or a motive. It sounds natural in academic essays and analytical journalism.
x: A simple idea underlies the whole design: nothing should be wasted.
Fear of failure may underlie his refusal to apply for promotion.

occupy.n: It has three main families of meaning. First, to fill or take up space or time: the museum occupies an entire block, the project occupied her all summer. Second, to live in or use a building or seat, so the flat is occupied or the seat is occupied. Third, to take over a place by force, as an army occupies a country. Be occupied with means be busy with. The noun occupation can mean a job or such a takeover.
x: The company will occupy three floors of the building in the city centre.
Hobbies occupy the children during the long school holidays.

manual.n: As an adjective, manual describes work or operation done by hand rather than by machine or automatically: manual labour, a manual gearbox, manual override. It does not carry a negative judgement by itself, but manual worker can imply physical, lower-paid jobs. Manual is also a noun for an instruction book, as in the user manual. Its opposite in this sense is automatic. The adverb is manually.
x: She drives a manual car, so she changes gear herself.
Farm work in the region is still largely manual, with few machines.

obtain.n: A formal alternative to get, used for things achieved through effort, request or process: obtain a visa, obtain consent, obtain results. In everyday speech get is more natural, and obtain can sound stiff in casual conversation. It is a transitive verb that takes a direct object. It can also be used intransitively in very formal writing to mean to exist or be in force, as in the conditions that obtain, but this is rare.
x: You must obtain a licence before you can sell food at the market.
The researchers obtained their data from hospital records over ten years.

orient.n: Pronounced ORI-ent as a verb, it means to direct something towards a goal or audience. It is mostly seen as a participle: the course is oriented towards, and in compounds such as customer-oriented or market-oriented. Orient yourself means to find your position or get used to a new place. Orientate has the same meaning but is mainly British and slightly wordier. The related noun is orientation, and the Orient is a dated word for East Asia.
x: The school is trying to orient its teaching towards real-world problems.
A small map helped the tourists orient themselves in the old town.

co-signer.n: A co-signer signs a loan, lease or contract together with the main borrower and promises to pay if that person does not. The term is common in American English for rental and student loans. In British English guarantor is the usual word. The verb is to co-sign, and the word is often written with a hyphen, though cosigner also occurs. Being a co-signer is a serious commitment, as the bank can ask you for repayment.
x: The landlord asked for a co-signer because Mia had just started her first job.
My uncle agreed to be a co-signer on the car loan.

colonise.n: To establish control over a territory by settling people there, usually in the context of empires: European powers colonised large parts of Africa. It can also describe plants, animals or bacteria spreading into a new area, and in science fiction it refers to settling planets. British spelling is colonise and American is colonize; the noun is colonisation or colonization. A colony is the place, and a colonist the person who settles.
x: Rabbits quickly colonised the island after sailors released them there.
Spain colonised much of South America in the sixteenth century.

debatable.n: Describes a claim or question on which reasonable people disagree, so it is not settled. It is milder and more polite than wrong: saying a point is debatable invites discussion. Common frames are it is debatable whether and highly debatable. It does not mean that something is being debated at that moment, only that it could be. Close in meaning are arguable and questionable; questionable often suggests doubt about quality or propriety.
x: It is debatable whether homework actually improves results for young children.
That the film is the director's best work is highly debatable.

epidemic.n: An epidemic is a rapid spread of an infectious disease in one community or region. It is wider than an outbreak, which can be small, and narrower than a pandemic, which spreads across many countries or continents. Stress is on the second syllable: ep-i-DEM-ic. It is also used figuratively for any harmful problem that spreads fast, as in an epidemic of obesity or loneliness. Verbs: spread, contain, trigger, and the epidemic peaks.
x: The city closed its schools to slow the cholera epidemic.
Some doctors describe loneliness among older people as a quiet epidemic.

figure out.n: A common phrasal verb meaning to understand or solve something after thinking about it. It is separable: figure the answer out or figure out the answer, and with a pronoun you must say figure it out. It often takes a wh-clause: figure out what went wrong, figure out how to. The register is informal to neutral. Especially common in American English; British speakers often prefer work out.
x: Nobody could figure out why the lights kept going off at night.
I will figure out the settings after watching a short tutorial.

fundraiser.n: Two meanings share the form. The more frequent is an event held to raise money for a cause, such as a charity dinner, a bake sale or a sponsored run. It can also mean the person whose job is to collect donations. Context decides. The collocations are hold, organise or host a fundraiser, and a fundraiser for something. In British English, fundraising event is also heard, and the verb is raise funds or fundraise.
x: Our class is organising a fundraiser to buy books for the village school.
She works as a fundraiser for a children's hospital.

habitat.n: The natural environment where a particular plant or animal normally lives, such as a rainforest, wetland or coral reef. It refers to the type of place, not to a single animal's home, so a nest or a den is different. Typical partners are natural habitat, loss of habitat and protect habitats. The plural is regular: habitats. Stress is on the first syllable: HAB-i-tat. It appears constantly in biology and conservation texts.
x: Wetlands provide a vital habitat for migrating birds.
Pandas are struggling because their bamboo forest habitat keeps shrinking.

hybrid.n: In biology, a hybrid is the offspring of two different species or varieties, like a mule. The word is also used far more widely for anything that combines two types, such as a hybrid car with a petrol engine and an electric motor, or hybrid working that mixes office and home days. It can be a noun (a hybrid) or an adjective (a hybrid model). Stress falls on the first syllable: HY-brid.
x: Gardeners often buy a hybrid tomato because it resists disease better.
My firm now offers hybrid working, with three days in the office.

jargon.n: Specialised vocabulary used within a profession or group that outsiders find hard to follow. It is usually uncountable and often mildly negative, implying that the language is unnecessarily complicated. People talk about legal, medical or business jargon, and ask a writer to avoid jargon. Jargon is not the same as slang, which is informal language linked to a social group, and a neutral word for specialised words is terminology.
x: The contract was so full of legal jargon that I needed help to read it.
Try to explain the idea without jargon so everyone can follow.

landlord.n: The person or company that owns a property and rents it to tenants. The female form is landlady. In British English, a landlord can also run a pub. The opposite is tenant. Common phrases are the landlord and tenant relationship, a private landlord and a social landlord, which is a housing association or council.
x: Our landlord has agreed to repaint the flat before we move in.
The landlord must give tenants written notice before raising the rent.

light-year.n: A light-year is a unit of distance, not of time: about 9.46 trillion kilometres, the distance light covers in one year in a vacuum. Astronomers use it for distances between stars and galaxies. It is a countable noun written with a hyphen, and it takes a plural, as in five light-years away. Figuratively, light-years away or ahead means very far behind or ahead in development, which is informal.
x: The galaxy is about two million light-years from Earth.
Their technology is light-years ahead of what their competitors can offer.

long-standing.n: An adjective meaning that has existed or continued for a long time, usually used of relationships, problems, traditions or disputes: a long-standing friendship, a long-standing rule. It is often positive for relationships and neutral or negative for problems. Usually before a noun, but also after be (the dispute is long-standing). Its meaning is close to established, but it stresses the length of time. Long-term refers to the future, not the past.
x: The two countries have a long-standing dispute over the border.
He is a long-standing member of the local sailing club.

magnificent.n: A strong adjective of praise for something impressive in size, beauty or quality: a magnificent castle, a magnificent performance. It is stronger than very good or beautiful, so it fits grand scenes more than everyday objects. It is used in both spoken and written English, though somewhat formal. The noun is magnificence, and the adverb is magnificently.
x: From the hilltop we had a magnificent view of the whole valley.
The orchestra gave a magnificent performance of Beethoven's ninth symphony.
